claim: Paratrechina longicornis is an invasive species with a broad worldwide distribution.
source: P. longicornis ants (McCreery and Breed, 2014; Czaczkes and Ratnieks, 2013; Gelblum et al., 2015), an invasive species with a broad worldwide distribution (Wetterer, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wetterer, 2008.

claim: The first recruiter ant deposits pheromone marks that span an entire path between the food and the nest.
source: A typical recruitment run. The first recruiter deposits a sequence of pheromone marks (blue dots) that span an entire path between the food (ring) and the nest.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1A which shows the trajectory and marks of the first recruiter ant.

claim: The recruitment trip spans the full distance to the nest at six meters, which is 2000 folds the body length of the ants.
source: This recruitment trip spans the full distance to the nest (N = 12 out of 12 ants at six meters, 2000 folds the body length of the ants)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 12 ants.

claim: The recruitment trip is characterized by a highly punctuated motion that was previously associated with pheromone laying behavior.
source: This recruitment trip spans the full distance to the nest (N = 12 out of 12 ants at six meters, 2000 folds the body length of the ants) and is characterized by a highly punctuated motion (Figure 1B) that was previously associated with pheromone laying behavior (Holldobler and Wilson, 1990; Beckers et al., 1992a; Hölldobler et al., 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1B showing speed profiles and by citations to previous work.

claim: Dips in the ant's speed can be related to marking events in which the ant touches the tip of its gaster to the surface.
source: Using a side-view camera we could indeed relate dips in the ant's speed with marking events in which the ant touches the tip of its gaster to the surface, a known property of marking behavior in various ant species (Beckers et al., 1992a; Hölldobler et al., 1978; Czaczkes et al., 2013a; Holldobler, 1981) (Figure 1C, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by side-view camera observations shown in Figure 1C and Video 1, and by citations to previous work.

claim: The identified marking events are accompanied by the deposition of undecane, a prominent P. longicornis trail pheromone.
source: Chemical analysis of the marked surfaces ascertains that the identified events are accompanied by the deposition of undecane, a prominent P. longicornis trail pheromone (Morgan et al., 2005; Witte et al., 2007a; Witte et al., 2007b) (Figure 1D–E, Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical analysis data shown in Figure 1D-E and by citations to previous work.

claim: Undecane has an extremely short lifetime due to fast evaporation.
source: The fast evaporation of this short hydrocarbon dictates an extremely short lifetime (Czaczkes and Ratnieks, 2013; Fujiwara-Tsujii et al., 2006) in comparison to most other pheromones found in the trails of other ant species (Morgan, 2009; Jackson et al., 2006; Beugnon and Déjean, 1992)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on undecane evaporation.

claim: The high volatility of undecane makes it a prevalent ant alarm pheromone.
source: In fact, the high volatility of undecane makes it a prevalent ant alarm pheromone (Fujiwara-Tsujii et al., 2006; Blum, 1969; Lenz et al., 2013; Regnier and Wilson, 1968).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on undecane as an alarm pheromone.

claim: P. longicornis exhibits short lived attractive responses to undecane, on the order of one minute.
source: The behavioral response of P. longicornis to this pheromone has, accordingly, been demonstrated to elicit short lived attractive responses, on the order of one minute (Witte et al., 2007b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Witte et al., 2007b.

claim: The marking detection method has a 93% true positive rate and a 13.1% false-detection-rate.
source: The association between a specific speed signature and the lowering of the gaster enables the identification of marking events using a top view camera (93% true positives and a false-detection-rate of 13.1%, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 2 and Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by validation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: Many ants accompanying the load engage in marking behavior during cooperative transport.
source: A prominent characteristic of cooperative transport in P. longicornis ants is that a large fraction of ants accompany the load rather than physically carry it (Czaczkes et al., 2013b). Our detection method reveals that many of these ants engage in marking behavior (Figure 1F), collectively laying scent marks with a mean rate of 1.4 marks per second (T = 785 s) in the vicinity of the load.
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 1F and quantitative measurements.

claim: Ants collectively lay scent marks with a mean rate of 1.4 marks per second in the vicinity of the load.
source: Our detection method reveals that many of these ants engage in marking behavior (Figure 1F), collectively laying scent marks with a mean rate of 1.4 marks per second (T = 785 s) in the vicinity of the load.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements over 785 seconds.

claim: When ants were prevented from obtaining information about the location of the nest, marking rates were significantly lower at 0.001 marks per second.
source: We found that when ants were prevented from obtaining information about the location of the nest (see the Experimental setup subsection of the Materials and methods), marking rates were significantly (p<10-4 unpaired T-test, T = 978 s) lower at 0.001 marks per second.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance testing.

claim: Scent marks convey navigational information.
source: This suggests that scent marks convey navigational information.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that marking rates decrease when ants lack nest location information.

claim: In obstacle free environments, markings hold accurate information (1.39 ± 0.02 bits per mark) regarding the direction to the nest.
source: Indeed, we find that, in obstacle free environments, markings hold accurate information (1.39 ± 0.02 bits per mark, N = 1395, see Materials and methods) regarding the direction to the nest (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative information theory analysis of 1395 marks shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Each new mark transfers 0.35 ± 0.02 bits of directional information to the team of carriers.
source: We find that, on average, each new mark transfers 0.35 ± 0.02 bits of directional information to the team of carriers, information that causes the group to divert the load's motion towards the mark (Figure 2B–C, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative information theory analysis shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Near an obstacle, markings that are directed towards the nest may form misleading trails that are inaccessible to large loads.
source: While the high directional accuracy of scent marks is typically advantageous, it may occasionally play a negative role in ragged environments which naturally contain obstacles. Near an obstacle, markings that are directed towards the nest may form misleading trails that are inaccessible to large loads (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 2D of natural environments.

claim: The gap between the perspective of an ant and the relevant information required by the group can lead to misleading trails.
source: This could arise from the inherent gap between the perspective of an ant (Von Uexkull, 1957) and the relevant information that is required by the group (Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by Video 6 showing ants passing obstacles that the load cannot, and by citation to Von Uexkull's concept of Umwelt.

claim: The ant-load system readily abandons the scent trail on a length scale as short as 10 cm.
source: Surprisingly, despite the fact that the ant-load system generally follows the scent trail (Figure 2B–C), we observe that it readily abandons it (Figure 3A) on a length scale that is as short as 10 cm (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 3A and quantitative analysis in Figure 3B.

claim: The locally-blazed trail behavior significantly deviates from classical trail following behavior exhibited by numerous ant species.
source: This behavior significantly deviates from classical trail following behavior as exhibited by numerous ant species as well as P. longicornis itself in other scenarios (see Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At most 10% of P. longicornis ants walking along a classical trail lose the trail.
source: Of the P. longicornis ants walking along a 'classical trail', at most 10% of them lose the trail which remains stable over time (up to several days) and over long distances.
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data on classical trail following.

claim: In the locally-blazed trail, the probability that the moving load approaches a scent mark continuously diminishes with distance.
source: Conversely, in the locally-blazed trail the probability that the moving load approaches a scent mark continuously diminishes with distance so that segments of the trail marked even slightly away of the object become practically irrelevant to subsequent movement.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fast evaporation of undecane is in agreement with the observation that the load abandons the trail after short distances.
source: We note that this observation is in agreement with the fast evaporation of undecane (Witte et al., 2007b).
evidence: The claim is an inference connecting the chemical properties of undecane to the observed behavior, supported by citation.

claim: The transported load leaves misleading scent marks and commences a perpendicular motion along and eventually around an obstacle.
source: We find that rather than being caught in a deadlock, the transported load leaves the misleading scent marks and commences a perpendicular motion along, and eventually around, the obstacle (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The vast majority of individual ants deposit markings in bouts which originate near the load, are directed towards the nest, and terminate a short distance away.
source: Indeed, we find that the vast majority of individual ants deposit markings in bouts which originate near the load (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), are directed towards the nest (Figure 2A) and terminate a short distance away (Figure 3D) much before they get anywhere near the nest (which is several meters away).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A, Figure 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The median bout length is less than 10 cm with a 95% confidence interval of [8.6 cm, 10.3 cm].
source: This locality of scent laying, with a median bout length of less than 10 cm (95% confidence interval is [8.6 cm, 10.3 cm] as estimated by a non-parametric Binomial-based method over N = 735 marking bouts)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of 735 marking bouts.

claim: The marking bout length stands in stark contrast to the 600 cm trail laid by the first recruiter ant.
source: This locality of scent laying, with a median bout length of less than 10 cm (95% confidence interval is [8.6 cm, 10.3 cm] as estimated by a non-parametric Binomial-based method over N = 735 marking bouts), stands in stark contrast to the 600 cm trail laid by the first recruiter ant (see the section titled Identification of pheromone deposition events, above) (p<10−6 probability that first ant marking distances come from the distribution depicted in Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison with p<10^-6.

claim: The locally-blazed trail is segmented and continuously formed in the vicinity of the object such that it implies only the next step to be taken.
source: First, rather than designating the whole route between the food and the nest (Hölldobler et al., 1978; Cammaerts and Cammaerts, 1980) (or any other two stable points that are, in no sense, required to be proximal [Latty et al., 2011]); the locally-blazed trail is segmented and continuously formed in the vicinity of the object such that it implies only the next step to be taken.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with classical trails cited in the literature and by the data presented earlier.

claim: As the load occasionally deviates from the trail, another trail dynamically forms in front of it.
source: Second, as the load occasionally deviates from the trail another trail dynamically forms in front of it. This happens in open space (Figure 3A) as well as near an obstacle (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3C.

claim: The length scales of the deviation from the scent trail and the marking bout length both match and are on the order of 10 cm.
source: Interestingly, the length scales of the deviation from the scent trail and the marking bout length both match and are on the order of 10 cm, possibly reflecting an evolutionary dependency between the two.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 3B and Figure 3D, with speculation about evolutionary significance.

claim: The Probabilistic-Following algorithm allows for asymptotically optimal (linear speed) travel times in 2D graphs provided that advice error rates are sufficiently small.
source: Adapting results from the theory of Random Walks in Random Environments (Drewitz et al., 2014; Sznitman, 2002), we prove that our model allows for asymptotically optimal (i.e. linear speed) travel times in 2D graphs (which are a good description of the world our ants live in) provided that advice error rates are sufficiently small (see Supplementary file 1-4).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical proof adapting results from Random Walks in Random Environments theory.

claim: Adding noise to the advice following rules is necessary and sufficient for efficient navigation on 2D graphs in the presence of occasionally misleading advice.
source: In other words, on these graphs and in the presence of occasionally misleading advice, adding noise to the advice following rules is not only necessary but also sufficient for efficient navigation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the theoretical proof described in the manuscript.

claim: The stretch is very low (under 3) over a large fraction of the parameter space which spans following probabilities between 0.5 and 0.9.
source: We find that the stretch is very low (under 3) over a large fraction of the parameter space which spans following probabilities between 0.5 and 0.9 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Probabilistic-Following is highly robust in the sense that it achieves near-optimal performance with hardly any requirement to fine-tune its parameters to the statistics of the environment.
source: To summarize, Probabilistic-Following is highly robust in the sense that it achieves near-optimal performance with hardly any requirement to fine-tune its parameters to the statistics of the environment. Such robustness and the generality which it implies are biologically appealing.
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The load travels almost ballistically in the absence of obstacles.
source: In the absence of obstacles, we have previously shown that, indeed, the load travels almost ballistically (Gelblum et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Gelblum et al., 2015.

claim: The motion of the load around the obstacle exhibits partial responsiveness to the underlying scent marks.
source: We further observe that the motion of the load around the obstacle exhibits partial responsiveness to the underlying scent marks (see the trajectory as depicted in Figure 5B) thus validating the assumptions of our model.
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The mean passage time scales linearly with obstacle width.
source: Taken together, the time saved near the slit outweighs the time lost on the non-productive detour and the load rapidly circumvents the obstacle. As predicted by our model, this motion is near-optimal in the sense that the mean passage time scales linearly with obstacle width (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the enclosed configuration where all scent marks mislead the carrying ants towards the slit, the time it takes the group to travel away from the slit scales exponentially with distance.
source: We find that, in this case, in agreement with the model's predictions, the time it takes the group to travel away from the slit scales exponentially with distance (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Scent marking and scent following are crucial components in the obstacle circumvention process.
source: While these interactions may induce some perpendicular motion (see Figure 3C) our result shows that, in general, this is insufficient to efficiently guide the group around the obstacle. Rather, scent marking and scent following are crucial components in this process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the stark contrast between linear and exponential traversal times in different scent mark configurations.

claim: The rate at which ants turn against pheromonal advice in the open-configuration experiment is, on average, once per 37.5 cm.
source: First, we estimate the rate at which the ants turn against pheromonal advice in the open-configuration experiment (see direction changes in Figure 5B) to be, on average, once per 37.5 cm (as measured over 15 trials and a total length of 636 cm).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from 15 trials over 636 cm.

claim: The correct relation between turning rate and exponential power holds for a persistence length of 7 cm and an 80% probability of following advice.
source: We find (see calculation in Supplementary file 1-5) that the correct relation between these values holds for a persistence length of 7 cm, in agreement with the 10 cm scale mentioned above, and an 80% probability of following advice, a value that lies well within the model's high efficiency zone (see Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations in Supplementary file 1-5 and comparison with Figure 4B.

claim: During the transport of small items, marking ants and carrying ants can traverse the same paths.
source: During the transport of small items marking ants and carrying ants can, to a large extent, traverse the same paths (it is often the case that laden ants concurrently mark the path).
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about ant foraging behavior.

claim: During cooperative transport, a passage that is open for a marking ant may be inaccessible for the larger load.
source: Simply put, in the context of cooperative transport, a passage that is open for a marking ant may be inaccessible for the larger load.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the scale differences between individual ants and the load.

claim: Scent marks deposited during the transport of small food items assist traffic between two stationary locations.
source: Scent marks deposited during the transport of small food items assist traffic between two stationary locations (e.g. the pile of seeds and the nest) (Franks et al., 1991; Bruce and Burd, 2012; Plowes et al., 2013; Bottinelli et al., 2015; Buhl et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on ant foraging trails.

claim: During cooperative transport, scent marks bridge between a fixed location (the nest) and a dynamically moving object (the carried load).
source: Conversely, during cooperative transport, scent marks bridge between a fixed location (the nest) and a dynamically moving object (the carried load).
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the nature of cooperative transport.

claim: The locally-blazed trail is morphologically distinct from previous descriptions of ant trails.
source: In light of these differences – we find that, during cooperative transport, ants employ a trail that is morphologically distinct from previous descriptions of ant trails.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript comparing the locally-blazed trail to classical trails.

claim: In classical ant trails, individual ants lay scent marks over long distances that are on the length scale of the distance to the nest.
source: Unlike classical ant trails where individual ants lay scent marks over long distances that are on the length scale of the distance to the nest (Cammaerts and Cammaerts, 1980; Beckers et al., 1992b), here, marking ants indicate only the next step to be taken (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on classical ant trails.

claim: Classical ant trails are typically clearly bounded and narrow due to relatively strict following of scent marks by ants.
source: Second, classical ant trails are typically clearly bounded and narrow. This is a result of the relatively strict manner in which ants follow the scent marks (Bruce and Burd, 2012; Eidmann, 1927; Carthy, 1951) which dominates over a secondary stochastic process where some ants distributively and individually wander off the trail (Beekman and Dussutour, 2007; Deneubourg et al., 1983; Perna et al., 2012; Gordon, 1995; Goss et al., 1989; Reid et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on classical ant trail following behavior.

claim: The locally-blazed trail does not have well defined boundaries due to repeated occasions in which the entire group of carrying ants collectively and simultaneously loses the trail.
source: The situation is very different for the locally-blazed trail which does not have well defined boundaries. This is a result of repeated occasions in which the entire group of carrying ants collectively and simultaneously loses the trail (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Stochastic components may grant search algorithms with the ability to escape from local minima.
source: In general, it is theoretically established that stochastic components may sometimes grant search algorithms with the ability to escape from local minima (Vermorel and Mohri, 2005; Selman et al., 1998; Kirkpatrick et al., 1983 ).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on stochastic optimization.

claim: Noisy trail following can resolve possible deadlocks when a high quality food source is introduced to ants that have already established a trail to a mediocre food source.
source: In particular, it has been shown that this principle is utilized by ants on classic foraging trails. In this case, noisy trail following can resolve possible deadlocks that may occur when a high quality food source is introduced to ants that have already established a trail to a mediocre food source (Beekman and Dussutour, 2007; Deneubourg et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on ant foraging behavior.

claim: The addition of noise cannot be considered as a silver-bullet that increases the efficiency of any search algorithm.
source: Indeed, the addition of noise cannot be considered as a silver-bullet that increases the efficiency of any search algorithm and there exist scenarios in which it simply does not work (Selman et al., 1998; Reingold, 2005; Patrascu and Thorup, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on algorithm design.

claim: A common strategy for reaching quality decisions in animal groups is to follow the majority.
source: To remain as a cohesive group, social animals have to take decisions collectively (Conradt et al., 2007). A common strategy for reaching quality decisions is to follow the majority (Ame et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on collective decision making.

claim: Majority based averaging mechanisms help groups reach accurate decisions even when individual perception is inaccurate and noisy.
source: Majority based averaging mechanisms have been shown to help the group reach accurate decisions even when its members' individual perception is inaccurate and noisy (Dell'Ariccia et al., 2008; Simons, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on collective decision making.

claim: Majority based decision making has been demonstrated to be helpful even in the context of conflict.
source: Majority based decision making has also been demonstrated to be helpful even in the context of conflict (Couzin et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Couzin et al., 2011.

claim: Animal groups have been shown to produce innovation even when this contradicts the natural tendencies to conform to the majority.
source: Animal groups have been shown to produce innovation even when this contradicts the natural tendencies to conform to the majority (Parrish, 1991; Reader and Laland, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on innovation in animal groups.

claim: The capacity for innovation has been observed in a diverse array of group living animals including fish, ants, mammals, and birds.
source: The capacity for innovation has been observed in a diverse array of group living animals including fish (Brown and Laland, 2002), ants (Beekman and Dussutour, 2007; Deneubourg et al., 1983; Czaczkes and Heinze, 2015), mammals (Reader and Laland, 2001, 2012), and birds (Rieucau and Giraldeau, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on various animal taxa.

claim: The noisy component of the locally blazed ant trail falls within the group of collective phenomenon involving innovation and exploration.
source: The noisy component of the locally blazed ant trail falls within this group of collective phenomenon.
evidence: The claim is an inference connecting the locally-blazed trail to the broader literature on collective innovation.

claim: The usefulness of noise and local exploration in animal groups extends beyond short time scales and single decisions and may be efficient for long time scales and multiple decisions.
source: Our work suggests that the usefulness of noise and local exploration in animal groups extends beyond short time scales and single decisions and may actually be efficient for the long time scales and multiple decisions that characterize any biological system.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Data was collected from six ant nests in Rehovot, Israel.
source: Data was collected from six ant nests in Rehovot, Israel.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental setup.

claim: Tests were carried out in the field during the summer when P. longicornis ants display cooperative transport behavior.
source: Tests were carried out, in the field, during the summer when P. longicornis ants display cooperative transport behavior.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental setup and timing.

claim: The marking detection procedure has identification rates of 93% of true positives and a positive likelihood ratio of 6.75.
source: We find that our method is highly reliable (Identification rates are 93% of true positives and a positive likelihood ratio of 6.75).
evidence: The claim is supported by validation data comparing top-view and side-view recordings.

claim: The probability that the marking bout distances of the first recruiter ant can be considered as samples of the distribution characterizing the locally-blazed ant trail is less than 10^-6.
source: The probability that the marking bout distances of the first recruiter ant can be considered as samples of the distribution characterizing the locally-blazed ant trail as depicted in Figure 3D was calculated by the probability of obtaining twelve independent samples of over six meters from this distribution. The probability of obtaining a single such sample is the number of measurements of six meters and over the total number of measurements which is p=16/735 ≈0.022. The probability of twelve consecutive such measurements is p12 < 10−6.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical calculation.
